title: Lattice Grid
context: Grade 4, and the chapter gives a second method for a job the first method already does. An adult sees a novelty. What the page is actually doing is separating the two halves of a long multiplication so that each can go wrong on its own: the grid holds every digit pair apart, and the strips put the places back together afterwards. The page's own claim about carrying is true of the first half and not the second, and its own worked example happens to need no pass to the left while all four questions printed beneath it do, so the sweep is taught here as part of the method rather than met by surprise.

writeup.why: Find a product a second way, by giving every pair of digits its own square and reading the answer off the diagonals.
writeup.look: A ruled grid of equal cells with a diagonal across each one, the digits of the two numbers outside it, and shaded strips running down to the bottom right corner.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Lattice Grid' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: how many cells the grid has and how many of them are filled, two numbers side by side in ink, so a grid that is one cell short can be read there without counting it over; on the last phase it carries how many strips have been swept and how many of them passed one to the left, written in words. Nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The grid bay is 620 by 440 at 64,202. The ruler control draws the lattice inside it as equal square cells at a pitch of 116, one column for each digit of the number along the top and one row for each digit of the number down the side, with a straight diagonal ruled corner to corner across every cell, all of them running the same way, and the whole grid centred in the bay at whatever size it comes out. The digits sit outside the grid and never inside it, the number along the top in deep blue above its columns and the number down the side in amber beside its rows; touching a cell lights the two digits it belongs to and dims nothing else. A cell takes two digits, one on each side of its diagonal, the tens digit in the upper half and the ones digit in the lower, and a pair coming to less than ten still fills both halves, with a grey zero in the upper one because that half is being held open. The answer rail is a single bent strip of empty squares 76 deep, running along the foot of the grid at 64,654 and turning up its left hand side, one square for every diagonal strip, and it fills from its right hand end as the sweep runs. The compare panel is 420 by 528 at 700,202 and holds the same product set out in columns: a heading row 36 tall of four ruled cells reading Th, H, T and O, a carry strip 34 tall above it where a carried digit stands small and vermilion above the column it is being added into, the multiplicand row 56 tall in deep blue, two partial product rows 56 tall in rose, a rule 4 tall and the product row 56 tall in green beneath it. The panel fills at the same pace as the grid, one column digit for every cell, so the rings arrive on one side of the working area while none arrive on the other. The sweep control then shades one diagonal strip at a time beginning at the bottom right corner, the shaded strip standing a shade darker than the paper and every other strip left exactly as it was; the strip's total is printed at its outer end as it shades, and where that total comes to more than nine the right hand digit drops into the answer rail and a small vermilion one travels up the strip and lands above the strip to its left, arriving there before that strip is totalled. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a cell or a strip total has to be written, with a thirteenth key that writes the grey zero for the upper half of a cell whose pair comes to less than ten. On the last phase a row of four place words, ones, tens, hundreds and thousands, sits under the keys and is printed again alongside the squares of the answer rail, because a strip is one place of the answer and a place holds a single digit. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the number being multiplied is deep blue, the number it is multiplied by is amber, the product under the rule is green, a digit carried into the next column is vermilion and is always drawn small above the column it joins, a partial product row made by one place of the multiplier is rose, and a zero holding a place open or a step that is skipped is grey. Chrome never borrows one of them, and every one of those readings survives with the colour taken away, because a column is told by the heading over it before it is told by its band, a carry is told by being small and sitting above the rule, and a row is told by the place named in the margin beside it.
writeup.finish: The card shows the grid the child filled with its strips still shaded and the product read off the edge beside it.

phases.win: the grid stands with one cell for every pair and a diagonal drawn across each one
phases.does: rules the grid to the size the two numbers ask for and sets the digits round its edges
phases.goal: the grid is ruled with one cell for each pair of digits and a diagonal in every cell
phases.says: Count the digits in each number. How many squares will the grid need?
phases.check: Away from the screen: you are to multiply a four digit number by a two digit number this way. How many cells does the grid need, and how many squares will the answer rail hold?
phases.feels: the grid looks like it is asking how many numbers there are, and it is really asking how many pairs of digits there are
phases.hands: Rule the grid with a ruler on squared paper, one square for every pair of digits, and draw all the diagonals the same way round before a single digit is written anywhere on it.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: how many digits has each of your two numbers? Second rung, the phase's: how many pairs can you make between them? Third rung: the digits step out one at a time and pair off on the stage while the empty grid redraws itself around them. The pad stays open behind all three.

wrong.why: a cell looks like a box for a number, and there are two numbers waiting to be put somewhere.
wrong.move: rules two cells because there are two numbers, so the grid for 87 x 35 comes out one cell across and two cells down.
wrong.screen: the digits step out of the two numbers one at a time and each pairs with every digit of the other, the pairings printed in a short list beside the bay: eight with three, seven with three, eight with five and seven with five, four of them for two digits against two. The grid redraws itself with one cell for each pairing and the list empties into it. Nothing is cleared and the answer stays in the slot.

wrong.why: every cell is drawn on its own, and a diagonal looks like that cell's own decoration rather than a piece of a line running through the whole grid.
wrong.move: rules the grid to the right size but draws each diagonal whichever way that cell happens to suggest, so some run down to the right and some down to the left.
wrong.screen: the sweep is tried and two strips cross in the middle of the grid, so one cell finds itself in two strips and another in none, and the answer rail is left with a square it cannot fill. The diagonals are then drawn again all running the same way and the strips lie parallel, each ending in its own square on the rail. Nothing is marked.

phases.screen: an empty stage with the two numbers waiting outside it and the ruler control lit
phases.soWhat: A lattice takes one cell for every pair of digits, so a three digit number against a two digit one wants six cells, and every cell carries a diagonal running the same way as all the others.
phases.concept: One cell for every pair of digits

phases.win: the cell fills on both sides of its diagonal and the next pair lights outside the grid
phases.does: multiplies the lit pair and writes the two digits on either side of the diagonal
phases.goal: each cell holds one digit fact with its tens above the diagonal and its ones below
phases.says: Tens above the line, ones below it. Every square takes two digits, even a small one.
phases.check: A cell pairs 4 and 2. What goes above its diagonal and what goes below it, and why is the upper half not left empty?
phases.feels: a square with one line through it turns out to be two places rather than one, and even a small product needs both of them
phases.hands: Fill one cell at a time on paper, saying the pair's product aloud as two digits even when it is a small one, so eight is said as zero and eight before it is written down.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what does that pair of digits come to? Second rung, the phase's: which half of the cell is the tens half? Third rung: the cell is opened on its own with its two halves named above and below the diagonal, and the product is written into them one digit at a time. The pad stays open and nothing already written is taken away.

wrong.why: eight is one digit and the cell is one square, so writing one digit in it looks like the whole job, and which half it goes in never comes up.
wrong.move: gives a cell whose pair comes to less than ten a single digit, so 4 x 2 in the grid for 74 x 26 is written as a bare 8 with nothing beside it, and because the pen was coming down off the digit outside the grid the 8 lands above the diagonal. The sweep then reads 2644 instead of 1924.
wrong.screen: the cell is opened large on its own with its diagonal across it and its two halves named, the upper one for tens and the lower one for ones. Eight has no tens, so the upper half takes a grey zero and the eight drops into the lower half where it belongs. The two strips that cell sits in are then swept again with it filled properly, and the rail reads 1924. Nothing is cleared.

wrong.why: a number is read from the left and written from the left, and the lower half is the half the pen reaches first coming down off the digit outside the grid.
wrong.move: puts the tens digit below the diagonal and the ones digit above it in every cell, so 7 x 6 = 42 reads 2 above and 4 below, and the grid for 74 x 26 sweeps to 5182.
wrong.screen: one cell is opened large with its halves named and the places of the answer printed along the answer rail beside it. The upper half is shown to lie in the strip one place further left than the lower half of the same cell, which is why the tens belong up there. Every cell is turned the right way round in place, one at a time, and the grid sweeps to 1924.

phases.screen: the ruled grid with every cell empty and one pair of digits lit outside it
phases.soWhat: The tens digit of a cell's product goes above its diagonal and the ones digit below it, and every cell takes two digits even when the pair comes to less than ten.
phases.concept: The diagonal splits tens from ones

phases.win: the column sum shows its rings and the grid shows none of them while it is being filled
phases.does: compares the two and says what the grid never once asked for
phases.goal: filling the grid asks for no carrying at all, because every cell is one digit times one digit
phases.says: Compare the grid with the column sum. What did the grid never ask you to do while you were multiplying?
phases.check: Fill the grid for 96 x 36 and count the carries. Then work 96 x 36 in columns and count them again. Which half of the work does the claim printed on the page actually cover?
phases.feels: the grid really does ask for no carrying while you multiply, and then the adding turns up and wants one after all
phases.hands: Work the same product twice on paper, once in the grid and once in columns, and put a ring round every carried digit in the column working before either answer is read out.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: what is the most a single cell's pair can come to? Second rung, the phase's: where do that product's tens go? Third rung: the grid and the column working are stood side by side and filled at the same pace, so the rings arrive on one side and not on the other while both are being multiplied. Nothing is marked.

wrong.why: a column sum sends whatever will not fit to the next column along, and a row of cells looks a great deal like a row of columns.
wrong.move: carries between cells while filling the grid, so a cell whose pair comes to 15 keeps its 5 and sends a 1 into the cell on its left.
wrong.screen: the cell is drawn large on its own with its diagonal across it, and the tens of its product are shown dropping into the upper half of that same cell rather than leaving it, because that half is where the cell keeps its own tens. The cells on either side are shown untouched throughout. Nothing is carried while you multiply your way across a grid, and the grid is then redrawn with every cell holding its own pair and no traffic at all between them.

wrong.why: the claim printed on the page stops at the word carrying, and a grid with every square full looks finished.
wrong.move: hears that nothing is carried while you multiply and takes it to mean nothing is left to do, so the filled cells are read straight off from the top left and a string of their digits is handed in.
wrong.screen: the word is split in two on the stage and each half is answered on its own. While you multiply, the grid asks for none, and that half is ticked off against the compare panel beside it. Then the strips are outlined as the second half of the job: they are the places of the answer and not one of them has been added yet. One strip shades from the bottom right corner to show what is still to come, and the cells stay exactly as the child left them.

phases.screen: the filled grid with the same product set out in columns beside it, its rings lit
phases.soWhat: Nothing is carried while I multiply through the cells, because each cell is one digit times one digit with its own half for its tens. That is the whole of what the claim covers, and the adding that comes after it is a separate matter.
phases.concept: Nothing is carried while you multiply

phases.win: every strip lands a digit, the ones that passed sit on the strips they joined, and the product reads off the edge
phases.does: sweeps each strip in turn from the bottom right corner and writes its digit
phases.goal: the strips are swept from the bottom right, and a strip past nine passes one to its left
phases.says: Start at the bottom right corner. If a strip comes to more than nine, pass one to the strip on its left.
phases.check: Sweep 84 x 56. Which strip passes one to its left, and what does the strip it lands on come to once that one has been counted in?
phases.feels: the grid was finished and there is a whole second job standing there, and the second job turns out to be adding
phases.hands: Sweep the strips on paper with a finger, one at a time from the bottom right corner, writing each strip's total out in the margin before any digit is written into the answer.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which corner does the sweep begin from? Second rung, the phase's: what does a strip do when it comes to more than nine? Third rung: the strips are shaded one at a time with each total printed at its outer end and the digit that travels drawn as it goes. Nothing on the grid is cleared.

wrong.why: the strip's total is a number and the square under it is where that strip's answer goes, and nobody has said that a square holds only one digit.
wrong.move: lets a strip that comes to ten put both its digits into one square of the answer rail, so 87 x 35 reads three, ten, four, five.
wrong.screen: the four squares of the rail are named with their places, ones, tens, hundreds and thousands, and the square holding ten is opened. A place holds a single digit, so the zero stays where it is and the one belongs to the place on its left. A small vermilion one lifts out of the square, travels up the strip and lands above the strip to its left, and that strip is totalled again with it counted in, giving three. The rail reads 3045.

wrong.why: a grid looks like something to be read, and reading starts at the top left of everything else in the book.
wrong.move: sweeps from the top left corner instead of the bottom right, because that is the corner a page is read from.
wrong.screen: the top left strip is shown to hold only the 2 from 3 x 8, and it is written as the first digit of the answer; two strips later one comes to ten and has nowhere to send its one, because the strip that should have taken it was written three moves ago. The answer rail is then named with its places, the bottom right corner is read as the ones place because it is the strip holding the two ones digits and nothing else, and the sweep is run again from there, the places climbing leftwards the way they do in every column working in the book.

phases.screen: the filled grid with the diagonal strips shaded and the answer squares empty down its edge
phases.soWhat: The strips are swept from the bottom right corner, each one is one place of the answer, and a strip coming to more than nine keeps its right hand digit and passes one to the strip on its left, which lands there before that strip is totalled.
phases.concept: The answer is read down the diagonals

writeup.delight: The third phase, the moment the grid and the column working finish together. The four cells of 87 x 35 fill one after another and not one ring appears anywhere on the grid, while an arm's length away in the compare panel the same product has drawn two of them in vermilion, each sitting small above the column it was joining. The two are left standing side by side for a beat. Then the sweep begins, and on the strip that comes to ten a vermilion one lifts off the grid for the first time and travels up to the strip on its left. The tool has been telling the truth in two halves, and the second half arrives with a ring of its own.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase the grid bay is empty paper with the two numbers waiting outside it, the one that will run along the top in deep blue and the one that will run down the side in amber, and the ruler control lit beneath them. On the second the grid is ruled and every cell is empty with its diagonal already drawn, and one pair of digits outside it is lit. On the third the grid stands full and the compare panel beside it holds the same product set out in columns, equally full, with its carry rings showing. On the fourth the grid is full, the diagonal strips are outlined but unshaded, and the answer rail runs empty along the foot and up the left hand side. The running count at the top left is empty and the slot and the pad stand empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the ruler control on the first phase, the lit pair of digits outside the grid on the second and third, or the bottom right corner of the grid on the last, gives one slow pulse while the voice says to rule the grid first. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any two numbers of two or three digits, with the ruler, the compare panel and the sweep open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on ruling the grid, filling a cell on both sides of its diagonal, scoping the claim the page makes, and sweeping the strips.
voiceLines: Rule the grid first. One square for every pair of digits, and a line across each.
Count the digits in each number. How many squares will the grid need?
Tens above the line, ones below it. Every square takes two digits, even a small one.
Compare the grid with the column sum. What did the grid never ask you to do while you were multiplying?
Start at the bottom right corner. If a strip comes to more than nine, pass one to the strip on its left.
A new pair of numbers. The grid changes size before anything else does.
Free play. Any two numbers, the ruler, the compare panel and the sweep all open.
Fill that square again and say which half each of its digits belongs in.
Every square held one fact on its own, and then the strips put the places back together.

observations.why: Every digit of one number has to meet every digit of the other exactly once, and the grid is built to make that unmissable.
observations.soWhat: I can count the cells I am going to need, and the squares the answer will fill, before I rule a single line.
observations.observe: The grid took one cell for every pair of digits, so a three digit number against a two digit one wanted six cells and a four digit against a two digit wanted eight.

observations.why: The upper half is the tens half, and a product below ten has no tens, which is exactly what a zero there says.
observations.soWhat: Every cell takes two digits, so every strip holds the same count of things and the sweep cannot quietly lose a place.
observations.observe: A pair coming to less than ten still filled both halves of its cell, with a grey zero sitting above the diagonal.

observations.why: Each cell holds one digit taken one digit of times, and the diagonal gives that product's tens their own half of the square instead of sending them next door.
observations.soWhat: Nothing is carried while I multiply through the cells, and that is exactly as far as the claim on the page reaches.
observations.observe: Filling all four cells of the grid for 87 x 35 asked for no carrying at all, while the same product set out in columns beside it drew two carry rings before its rows had even been added.

observations.why: Each strip is one place of the answer and a place holds a single digit, so whatever will not fit there belongs to the place above it.
observations.soWhat: The carrying the grid spared me while I was multiplying turns up again once the strips are added, and it always travels left, never right.
observations.observe: Sweeping 87 x 35 reached a strip holding four, four and two, which came to ten, so it wrote a zero, sent one to the strip on its left, and the rail read 3045.

description: Rule a grid with one cell for every pair of digits, fill each cell with a single digit fact split by its diagonal, then sweep the strips from the bottom right.

mods.practice: Practice, child alone. Eight items on ruling the grid, filling a cell on both sides of its diagonal, scoping the claim the page makes, and sweeping the strips.

source_tool.name: Lattice Grid
source_tool.blurb: Rule a grid with one cell for every pair of digits, fill each cell with a single digit fact split by its diagonal, then sweep the strips from the bottom right.

finding the product of fifty-seven and seventy-seven by lattice multiplication

source_tool.description: A ruler control draws the grid to whatever size the two numbers ask for, one cell across for each digit of the first number and one cell down for each digit of the second, with a straight diagonal across every cell all running the same way. The digits sit outside the grid, one number along the top and the other down the side, so every cell belongs to exactly one pair and the pair it belongs to lights when the cell is touched. Cells are filled one at a time: the pair multiplies, the tens digit goes above the diagonal and the ones digit below it, and a cell whose pair comes to less than ten still takes two digits, with a zero in its upper half. Because every cell is one digit times one digit, nothing at all has to be carried while multiplying, and a compare panel stands the same product in columns beside the grid with its rings lit so the difference can be seen rather than claimed. Then the sweep. The diagonal strips shade one at a time from the bottom right corner, each strip totals as it shades, and a strip that comes to more than nine keeps its right hand digit and passes one onto the strip to its left, which lands there before that strip is totalled. The digits read off the edge, back the way the sweep came, as the product.
source_tool.art_direction: A ruled grid with a diagonal everywhere / Picture book

style.text: Least text. One header line, short labels, nothing else. The voice carries the teaching and the caption carries the voice.

stage.note: Every coordinate is authored in 1600x900, so a smartboard and a phone in landscape get one composition. Nothing scrolls. The three bands below are the settled layout, taken from Two Hundred Trail in Class 3 chapter 3 once it was finished; a tool that has to depart from one of them says in its own writeup.stage which band it changed and why.

bands.canvas: 92 to 746. One rounded panel holding everything the child works on.
bands.footer: 758 to 900. The voice at the far left, the phase bar at the right.
bands.header: 0 to 80. One line, and only one.

zones.bar: the phase bar at the right of the footer, the question count under it
zones.pad: under the slot, and furniture on every phase: twelve keys three across where a number is asked for, a word pad where a name or a rule is
zones.name: the tool name at the far left of the header, a measured dot set clear of it
zones.runs: the running count, on the canvas at its top left, never up in the chrome. It counts the thing the tool is actually building; where a tool has nothing to count that corner carries the record being kept instead, and that tool's own stage says so
zones.slot: the question and the child's answer, fixed down the right of the canvas
zones.work: the working area, one thousand and eighty-six by five hundred and twenty-eight
zones.title: the phase title beside that dot, on the same single header line
zones.voice: the caption at the far left of the footer, its speaking dot beside it
zones.chrome: again, sound and restart, as round controls at the far right of the header

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: ruled column mats with a heading over every column, digit cards that can be picked up and dropped, place cards that split off a multiplier, trays that hold a number while it is taken several times, a table strip that grows a row at a time, and a ruled grid with a diagonal in every cell.

A multiplication set out in columns always shows its columns: one digit to a column, every column under its named heading, the rows aligned by their right ends, and a horizontal rule between the last row and the product. A bare row of digits with no column mat behind it is never used to teach multiplying.
A carried digit is always drawn small, inside a ring above the column it is being added into, never in the margin and never below the rule.
A partial product row is drawn with the place of the multiplier that made it named beside it, and with its trailing zeros written rather than implied.

A lattice is drawn as a true grid of equal square cells with one straight diagonal in every cell, all running the same way, the digits of the two numbers sitting outside the grid, and every cell holding two digits on either side of its diagonal even when the pair multiplies to less than ten, so that nothing has to be carried while multiplying.
Where tokens or groups stand for a quantity, exactly the stated number of them is drawn, every group holds the same count, they never overlap, and they stay countable at a glance.
A column is told apart by its heading first and by its band second, so the stage still reads with the colour taken away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a digit, a column, a cell or a token the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. The number being multiplied is deep blue, the number it is multiplied by is amber, and the product under the rule is green, and those three are the same three colours in every tool and every picture of this chapter. A digit carried into the next column is vermilion, so it is told apart from the digits it is joining. A partial product row, made by one place of the multiplier, is rose, so a row is read as a part before it is read as an answer. A zero holding a place open, and a place of the multiplier that is skipped, are both grey, because neither one is a quantity. All of that holds in greyscale, because a carried digit is told apart by being small and sitting in a ring above its column before it is told apart by its colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.
props.muted is honoured at the source, and turning sound off cancels any line already speaking.
voice.where: The caption line sits at the far left of the footer with a small dot beside it that glows while the voice is talking. An again control repeats the last line.
voice.figure: None. The voice speaks with nothing on the stage.
voice.onMiss: Fill that square again and say which half each of its digits belongs in.
voice.onNext: A new pair of numbers. The grid changes size before anything else does.
voice.opening: Rule the grid first. One square for every pair of digits, and a line across each.
voice.onFinish: Every square held one fact on its own, and then the strips put the places back together.
voice.onFreePlay: Free play. Any two numbers, the ruler, the compare panel and the sweep all open.
voice.figure_rule: A figure appears only where the printed chapter puts one and it has work to do. Everywhere else the voice speaks from the caption line with nothing on the stage: a mascot with no job is one more thing competing with the quantities the child is looking at.

The answer is read down the diagonals

placement.where: After the same product has been worked once in columns, so there is an answer to land on. The tool is what shades a single diagonal strip while the rest of the grid stands still, which a drawn page cannot.

answer_key.rule: Rule a grid one cell across for each digit of the first number and one cell down for each digit of the second, with a diagonal across every cell. Write one number along the top and the other down the side. Fill each cell with its pair's product, the tens digit above the diagonal and the ones digit below it, and give every cell two digits even when the pair comes to less than ten. Nothing is carried while you are multiplying, because each cell holds a single digit fact on its own. Then add along the diagonal strips, starting at the bottom right corner. A strip that comes to more than nine keeps its right hand digit and passes one onto the strip to its left, which is counted in before that strip is totalled. Read the digits back off the edge and that is the product.
answer_key.wrong: The strip unshades and is swept again slowly, its cells lighting one at a time as they join the total, with the digit that passes to the left drawn as it travels. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

hostProps.muted: Sound off. Honour it at the source, not by muting an element later. The captions carry on.
hostProps.phase: number, 1-based, which phase to build. The host chooses the activity; the component builds that phase and nothing else and never moves on by itself.
hostProps.device: tablet / web / smartboard. The stage is a fixed 1600x900 that scales; lay nothing out per device.
hostProps.audience: classroom or solo, and ACCEPTED AND NOT ACTED ON. The teach run and the hint ladder run either way. Kept so the contract is one shape across the book, and named here so nobody reads the shape as a promise.
hostProps.learnQuestions: The four worked items, one per phase, supplied by the host.
hostProps.practiceQuestions: The eight practice items, supplied by the host.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: 74 has two digits and 26 has two digits.
Every digit of the first pairs with every digit of the second, which makes four pairs.
So the grid is two cells across and two cells down, and each cell holds one pair's product.
items.answer: Four cells, one for each pair of digits
items.question: How many cells does a grid for 74 x 26 need, and what does each one hold?
items.checkpoint: Every pair of digits gets its own square, so none is missed and none is used twice.
items.misconception: Drawing two cells because there are two numbers, instead of one cell for every pair of digits.

steps: The upper row pairs with 2: 7 x 2 = 14, so 1 goes above the diagonal and 4 below it.
Still in that row, 4 x 2 = 8, so 0 goes above the diagonal and 8 below it, because every cell takes two digits.
The lower row pairs with 6: 7 x 6 = 42 gives 4 above and 2 below, and 4 x 6 = 24 gives 2 above and 4 below.
items.answer: 7 x 2 gives 1 and 4, 4 x 2 gives 0 and 8, 7 x 6 gives 4 and 2, and 4 x 6 gives 2 and 4
items.question: Fill the four cells of the grid for 74 x 26.
items.checkpoint: The tens digit of a cell's product goes above its diagonal and the ones digit below it.
items.misconception: Writing a single 8 in the cell for 4 x 2 and leaving the upper half of that cell empty.

steps: Each cell holds one digit of the first number taken one digit of the second number of times.
A cell product such as 42 does not overflow, because the diagonal gives its tens their own half of the square.
So nothing is carried while you multiply. What remains comes later, when the strips are added.
items.answer: Not once, because every cell is a single digit multiplied by a single digit
items.question: While the cells of the grid for 74 x 26 are being filled, how many times do you have to carry?
items.checkpoint: Nothing is carried while you multiply, which is what the grid is for, and the adding that follows is a separate matter.
items.misconception: Taking the claim further than it goes and expecting the diagonal strips to need no pass to the left either.

steps: Start at the bottom right. That strip holds 4 on its own.
The next strip holds 2, 2 and 8, which comes to 12, so 2 is written and one passes onto the strip to its left.
That strip holds 4, 0 and 4 with the one it was passed, which comes to 9, and the last strip holds 1, so the product reads 1924.
items.question: Sweep the diagonals of the grid for 74 x 26 and read off the product.
items.checkpoint: The strips are swept from the bottom right, and a strip past nine passes one to its left before that strip is totalled.
items.misconception: Writing 12 into the answer where a strip comes to twelve, instead of keeping 2 and passing one to the left.

items.question: A grid is ruled for a three digit number multiplied by a two digit number. How many cells does it have?
items.final_answer: Six, because each of the three digits pairs with each of the two

items.question: Where do the digits of the two numbers go on a grid like this one?
items.final_answer: One number along the top and the other down the side, so that every cell belongs to exactly one pair

items.question: A cell pairs 9 and 3. What goes above its diagonal and what goes below?
A cell pairs 4 and 2. What goes above its diagonal and what goes below?
items.final_answer: 0 above and 8 below, because 4 x 2 = 8 and every cell takes two digits

items.question: Why is nothing carried while you multiply your way through the cells?
items.final_answer: Because every cell is one digit times one digit, and the diagonal gives the tens their own half of the square

items.question: A child says this method never needs carrying. The claim holds while you are multiplying, so where does it break down?
items.final_answer: At the strips. When the diagonals are added, a strip that comes to more than nine still passes one to its left

items.question: Find 68 x 45 this way, and say which strip passed one to its left.
items.final_answer: 3060, and the third strip from the right came to 10, so it passed one to its left

items.question: Find 76 x 54 this way, and say how many strips passed one to the left.
items.final_answer: 4104, and two strips in a row passed one to the left

teaching_notes: Rule the grid with a ruler the first time and let it take as long as it takes. Drawn freehand it stops being a grid and the strips stop lining up. Work the chapter's own example all the way through before the tool is opened: 55 multiplied by 23 fills four cells, and the strips read five, six, two and one from the right, so the product is 1265. Then say the claim printed on that page carefully, because the page itself does not. Nothing is carried while you multiply, and that much is true: every cell is a single digit fact. The adding that follows is a different matter, and all four questions printed directly beneath that claim have a strip that comes to more than nine and has to pass one to its left. Work one of them with the class so the first pass happens where everybody can see it, and keep the sweep going strictly from the bottom right corner. Finish by working the same product in columns and standing the two answers together. A child who has seen both methods land on one number owns the second one instead of performing it.
generation_prompt: Build a grid multiplication tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A ruler control draws a true grid of equal square cells, one column per digit of the first number and one row per digit of the second, with a straight diagonal across every cell all running the same way. The digits sit outside the grid, one number along the top and one down the side, and touching a cell lights the row digit and column digit it belongs to. Cells fill one at a time with the pair's product, the tens digit written above the diagonal and the ones digit below it, and a pair coming to less than ten still fills both halves with a zero in the upper one. A compare panel stands the same product set out in columns beside the grid, with its rings lit, so the contrast is shown and not merely stated: while the grid is being filled nothing is carried, because every cell is a single digit fact. A sweep control then shades the diagonal strips one at a time beginning at the bottom right corner, totalling each strip as it shades; a strip past nine keeps its right hand digit and animates one travelling onto the strip to its left, landing there before that strip is totalled. The digits read off the edge in sweep order as the product. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Rule the grid first, one square for every pair of digits, with a diagonal in each. Write one number along the top and the other down the side. Fill each square with its pair, tens above the line and ones below. Then sweep the strips from the bottom right corner, and pass one to the left whenever a strip comes to more than nine.
